title: General defences may defeat or limit an otherwise established tort

content.overview: General defences may defeat or limit an otherwise established tort. Volenti, inevitable accident, act of God and necessity are distinct doctrines with different ingredients.
content.glance: General defences may defeat or limit an otherwise established tort. Volenti, inevitable accident, act of God and necessity are distinct doctrines with different ingredients.
content.study: General defences may defeat or limit an otherwise established tort. Volenti, inevitable accident, act of God and necessity are distinct doctrines with different ingredients.\n\nThe common law recognises circumstances where conduct is consented to, unavoidable, justified by extraordinary natural forces, or necessary to avert a greater danger. Volenti requires informed and voluntary assumption of risk; mere knowledge is not automatically consent. Necessity is narrowly framed and ordinarily requires proportionality.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: The common law recognises circumstances where conduct is consented to, unavoidable, justified by extraordinary natural forces, or necessary to avert a greater danger. Volenti requires informed and voluntary assumption of risk; mere knowledge is not automatically consent. Necessity is narrowly framed and ordinarily requires proportionality.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: These are common-law doctrines rather than one statutory code. Consent, necessity, statutory authority and other justifications must be analysed separately. A waiver is evidence of consent, not automatically conclusive in every case.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Identify the prima facie tort. 2. Identify the exact defence. 3. Prove every condition of that defence. 4. Test consent, necessity, foreseeability and proportionality as applicable.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: The defendant generally bears the evidentiary burden for a positive defence on the civil standard, subject to the procedural allocation applicable to the issue. Warnings, consent documents, weather records and expert evidence may be relevant.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Defences should be pleaded with particulars. The court identifies the cause of action before deciding whether the defence is available. Limitation follows the underlying claim.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Knowledge of risk is not necessarily voluntary assumption of risk; an inevitable accident may excuse liability where reasonable care could not prevent the event. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Consent must be informed, voluntary and directed to the relevant risk. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.

distinctions.title: Volenti vs Necessity
distinctions.right: Volenti rests on valid consent to risk; necessity rests on justification of interference to avert imminent harm.
